arguments.title: How to Prepare for a Bicycle Puncture Repair Visit
arguments.content:
A flat tire is easier to fix when you arrive with a little information ready. Our workshop repairs bicycle tire punctures and inspects tires, and the visit goes faster when you can describe what happened.

Here is what to gather before you bring the bike in.

Note when the air loss happens

Air loss patterns point to different causes. Try to recall which of these matches your bike:

  • The tire went flat suddenly while you were riding.
  • The tire goes soft over a few hours.
  • The tire goes soft over several days or weeks.
  • The tire only loses air after you pump it to a high pressure.

You do not need a diagnosis. Just describe the timing in your own words when you drop the bike off.

Remember where and how you were riding

The conditions before the flat are useful. Think about whether you hit a pothole or a kerb, rode over broken glass or gravel, or noticed the rim bottoming out. Also mention if the bike sat unused for a long stretch before the tire went soft.

Check whether the puncture has happened before

A repeat flat in the same wheel is worth flagging. Tell us how many times it has happened, whether it was always the same wheel, and whether anything was replaced or patched in between. A recurring flat often needs the tire, rim tape and rim inspected, not only the tube.

Bring the bike with the wheel still on

Bring the whole bike if you can. Customers are welcome to bring the bike in and describe when the air loss occurs. Leaving the wheel mounted lets us check the rim, the rim tape and the tire together, and it keeps the valve and brake setup as you have been riding it.

If you already removed the tube or the tire, bring those parts too. A used tube can show where the hole sits, which helps trace the cause.

Leave anything you found in the tire

If you pulled a thorn, staple, shard of glass or wire from the tread, keep it and hand it over. A recovered object confirms the entry point quickly.

Say how you use the bike

Your riding pattern affects what makes sense for the repair. Useful details include your usual route surface, whether you carry cargo or a child seat, roughly how far you ride in a normal week, and whether you have a preferred tire or tube already.

A short checklist

  • When the air loss starts and how fast it goes.
  • What you were riding on or over just before.
  • Whether this wheel has gone flat before.
  • Any object you removed from the tire.
  • Any parts you already replaced yourself.
  • How and where you normally ride.

Next step

Once you have those notes, bring the bike to the workshop. You can read more about what the service covers on our bicycle puncture repair page.

If you are not sure which tire your bike takes, our guide to reading tire size markings covers how to find that number on the sidewall.
